chunks: My father narrated to him, may God be pleased with him, saying: Sa'd ibn Abdullah narrated from Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Khalid, from his father, from Muhammad ibn Sinan, from Ibn Miskan, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said:

Indeed, the people most deserving to wish for others to be rich are the misers, because when people become rich, they refrain from spending their wealth (on others). And the people most deserving to wish for others to be righteous/perfect are those with faults, because when people are righteous, they refrain from seeking out the faults of others. And the people most deserving to wish for others to be forbearing/patient are those who are foolish, who need others to pardon their foolishness. So now, the misers wish for people to be poor, the fault-finders wish for people to have faults, and the foolish wish for people to be foolish. And in poverty is the need for the miser, and in corruption (of character) is the seeking of the defects of those with faults, and in foolishness is the requital (with) sins.
ai.seo_question: Why do misers wish for others to be poor according to Imam al-Sadiq?
ai.summary: In *Al-Khisal*, Shaykh al-Saduq records Imam al-Sadiq’s (a) psychological insight that those possessing a trait often wish for its absence in others to alleviate their own burden, yet misers, fault-finders, and the foolish paradoxically desire the persistence of their respective counterparts. This tradition highlights the spiritual stagnation of these groups, as their desires reinforce their flaws rather than seeking the relief that comes with the opposite state, a concept deeply rooted in Shia ethical discourse on self-awareness and character refinement.
